Getting started with the QuakeScope pick catalogues¶

Machine-learning P and S picks on continuous data, published as Parquet on S3. No credentials, no database, no account. Every cell below runs anonymously, on Colab or a laptop, in about ten minutes.

Three catalogues share one bucket, one layout and one schema, so the same reader works for all of them:

prefix picker and weights years station-locations (with picks) rows in the Parquet stored
western/ PhaseNet, original weights (Zhu and Beroza, 2019), P and S thresholds 0.2 1986 to Sep 2026 26,377 (12,981) 2,130,446,013 (~2.07 B unique) 55.3 GB
obs/ PickBlue (Bornstein et al., 2024), PhaseNet architecture, thresholds 0.2 1993 to 2026 3,036 offshore (2,001) 104,420,230 (~103.6 M unique) 2.9 GB
quakescope-2025/ PhaseNet, instance weights, thresholds 0.2: the picks of Ni et al. (2025, Seismica) 2002 to Mar 2025 58,403 4,376,745,115 88.3 GB

Sources: 2026 rows are the sum of num_rows over every Parquet footer, read on 2026-10-13 (_archive/inventory-20261013/, also on the western and obs report pages); the "unique" estimate is explained in section 2. The 2025 count is the exporter's per-network row count, equal to the retired DocumentDB database's count for all 453 networks (2026-10-14). Stored sizes are an S3 listing of 2026-10-19, which also shows nothing written to western/ since 2026-10-10 or to obs/ since 2026-10-09.

This notebook:

  1. reads the three station tables and maps them,
  2. mirrors one month of one network from western and de-duplicates it,
  3. asks the availability table which station-days were read, and which had data but no picks,
  4. reads the same month from the 2025 catalogue and compares the two pick sets, station-day by station-day and pick by pick,
  5. fetches the waveforms from FDSN and draws both catalogues' picks on them,
  6. reads a month of ocean-bottom picks (the Alaska Amphibious Community Seismic Experiment, AACSE),
  7. reads the run records that say which model produced each pick,
  8. shows how to read at scale.

For a region and a period, coverage maps and export for PyOcto or GaMMA, continue with download_the_catalogue.ipynb. Reference: docs/data_access.md.

If you pulled picks before October 2026¶

change date what to do
Utah, Montana, Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, BC, Alberta, Baja California and Sonora stations added (western-fill, western-fill2) 2026-10-02 re-sync the networks you use
start_date / end_date are Parquet dates; the old YYYY.DDD floats stay as start_yearday / end_yearday 2026-09-29 re-read stations.parquet
15.6 M western station-days re-read (western-reread2): the reader had chosen one band per station for the whole campaign and skipped days without it; it now picks the best band present each day 2026-10-06 to 10-09 re-sync; this is where most new picks are
availability table, one row per station-day (<catalogue>/availability/) 2026-10-09 use it instead of the manifests (section 3)
interrupted shard attempts left about 64 M duplicate rows in western measured 2026-10-13 de-duplicate on (tid, cha, pha, peak) (section 2)
the 2025 instance catalogue converted to the same Parquet layout 2026-10-14 section 4
obs holds offshore stations only (land stations had come in through reused temporary network codes) 2026-10-03 re-sync obs

Safe to re-run; skip the install if you already have these.

In [2]:
import datetime as dt, json, time, urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import s3fs

BUCKET = "quakescope-picks-2026"
ANON = {"anon": True}               # public-read: no keys, no config, no account
fs = s3fs.S3FileSystem(anon=True)
HTTPS = f"https://{BUCKET}.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com"

MIRROR = Path("quakescope_mirror")  # local copy, same layout as the bucket
MIRROR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

KEY = ["tid", "cha", "pha", "peak"]  # one pick; rows repeating it are duplicates (section 2)
C26, C25, C_OBS = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1b9e77"
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})


def mirror(catalogue, net, year, month):
    # Copy one partition down, skipping files already present. Returns the local directory.
    prefix = f"{catalogue}/picks/network={net}/year={year}/month={month:02d}/"
    local = MIRROR / prefix
    local.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    try:
        remote = fs.ls(f"{BUCKET}/{prefix}", detail=True)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        remote = []
    todo = [o["name"] for o in remote if not (local / Path(o["name"]).name).exists()]
    t0 = time.time()
    if todo:
        fs.get(todo, [str(local / Path(k).name) for k in todo])
    print(f"{prefix}: {len(remote)} files, {sum(o['size'] for o in remote) / 1e6:.0f} MB, "
          f"{len(todo)} fetched in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")
    return local


def read_picks(local):
    # Read a mirrored partition and drop duplicate rows (same station, band, phase and time).
    df = pd.read_parquet(local)
    n = len(df)
    df = df.drop_duplicates(KEY).reset_index(drop=True)
    print(f"{n:,} rows, {n - len(df):,} duplicates dropped, {len(df):,} picks")
    return df

1. The station tables¶

stations.parquet is the table each campaign was planned from: every station-location with coordinates, the bands the archive lists, and the operating window. It is the index for choosing what to read.

Join on id, which equals the picks' tid (NET.STA.LOC, location code possibly empty: CI.CLC.). Take network, station and location from id.split("."): the separate code columns of the 2026 tables still carry CSV-parse damage in places (1.0 where the location code is 01; 2,065 western rows on 2026-10-19). start_date and end_date are Parquet dates in the 2026 tables; a station still operating carries 3000-01-01, not a null.

In [3]:
tables = {c: pd.read_parquet(f"s3://{BUCKET}/{c}/stations.parquet", storage_options=ANON)
          for c in ("western", "obs", "quakescope-2025")}
# The 2025 table keeps the database's "YYYY.DDD" strings (always three digits after the point,
# "2019.227"), so they parse safely; the 2026 tables already hold Parquet dates.
q = tables["quakescope-2025"]
for col in ("start_date", "end_date"):
    q[col] = q[col].map(lambda s: dt.datetime.strptime(s, "%Y.%j").date())   # 3000.001 is beyond pandas timestamps

for c, s in tables.items():
    nets = s.id.str.split(".").str[0]
    print(f"{c:16s} {len(s):6,} station-locations in {nets.nunique():3d} networks")

The 2025 table is global and lists every location code the metadata ever declared; the 2026 western table covers the western states and their neighbours, including stations whose data start before 2002 (the 2025 run began in 2002, the 2026 run in 1986).

2. One month of picks, de-duplicated¶

The catalogue is Hive-partitioned by network / year / month. The fast way to read a partition is to copy it down, then read it locally: a month mirrors in seconds and reads in under one, against a minute and a half read straight from S3 file by file.

The example is the Southern California network CI in July 2019, the month of the Ridgecrest sequence.

In [5]:
NET, YEAR, MONTH = "CI", 2019, 7
w_local = mirror("western", NET, YEAR, MONTH)
picks = read_picks(w_local)

4 CI.CPO. EH P 2019-07-03 01:13:58.830 2019-07-03 01:13:58.930 2019-07-03 01:13:59.080 0.323469 NaN 0.000029 81932ad1-5feb-4024-97ec-f5c1d9722d0e

Why there are duplicates. Workers ran on Spot capacity. When AWS reclaimed one mid-shard, its partial output stayed in the bucket and the shard was run again from the start, so some picks were written twice, with different run ids (rid). The picker is deterministic (re-picking through ObsPy/FDSN on another architecture reproduced 59,298 of 59,315 picks to the millisecond, western_pick_validation), so a repeated (tid, cha, pha, peak) is the same pick. On 2026-10-13, 12,125 western objects (69.7 M rows) were listed by no manifest; in a sample of 200 of them 92.2 % of rows repeated a pick in a listed object, about 64 M duplicates in all. They will be removed from the bucket; until then, drop them when you read.

The columns¶

column meaning
tid NET.STA.LOC; joins to stations.id
cha the band picked that station-day (HH, EH, BH, HN, ...). In 2026, one band per station-day: the first of HH > EH > SH > BH > BN > DP > HN > CN present in that day's data (obs adds EL). In 2025, every band was picked separately
pha P or S
start, peak, end the probability window, millisecond resolution; peak is the arrival time
conf peak probability, 0 to 1; everything at or above 0.2 is stored
amp Wood-Anderson displacement (m), response removed, mean of the horizontals; only for conf >= 0.5. 2025 used damping h = 0.8, 2026 uses 0.7
amp_vel peak ground velocity near the pick (m/s), counts over the instrument sensitivity, high-passed; on about 99 % of 2026 picks, empty in 2025
rid run id, resolves to <catalogue>/runs/<rid>.json
network, year, month partition keys, read from the path

conf is a detection score, not a probability that the pick is right. 0.2 is deliberately permissive; choose your floor on your own target events. The weights put their scores on different scales, so the same number means different things in the 2025 and 2026 catalogues (section 4).

P and S should track each other day by day; a day where one collapses is usually a data outage, not a quiet Earth. The step on July 4 and 6 is the Ridgecrest M6.4 foreshock and M7.1 mainshock.

3. Was each station-day read? The availability table¶

A station-day with no picks can mean three different things: the archive held no data, the data held no arrival above 0.2, or the campaign never read it. <catalogue>/availability/network=<NET>/availability.parquet says which, one row per station-day inside each station's operating epochs, built from every job manifest.

status meaning
loaded read and picked; npks is the pick count, and npks = 0 means data with no arrival above 0.2
no_data the archive listing held nothing that day
not_found the archive has no such network-year
empty_read an object exists but holds no pickable band (detail says what it holds)
unread attempted and not read (detail: e.g. too_big)
unknown inside the station's epochs, no record either way (mostly older shards that recorded only what they read, the strong-motion network NP, and networks our account cannot read)
In [8]:

# The table and the Parquet should agree: a loaded station-day with npks > 0 has picks.
got = picks.groupby(["tid", picks.peak.dt.floor("D").rename("date")]).size().rename("n_parquet").reset_index()
loaded = month[month.status == "loaded"]
chk = loaded.merge(got, on=["tid", "date"], how="left").fillna({"n_parquet": 0})
print(f"loaded station-days with npks > 0: {(chk.npks > 0).sum():,}; of those, with picks in the Parquet: "
      f"{((chk.npks > 0) & (chk.n_parquet > 0)).sum():,}")
outside = got.merge(loaded[["tid", "date"]], how="left", indicator=True)
outside = outside[outside["_merge"] == "left_only"]
print(f"picks on station-days the table does not call loaded: {int(outside.n_parquet.sum()):,} "
      f"on {len(outside):,} station-days")

no_picks = month[(month.status == "loaded") & (month.npks == 0)].tid.value_counts()
print(f"\nstations with data but no picks on some days this month: {len(no_picks)}")
print(no_picks.head(8).to_string())

Two things to take from the check. Every station-day the table calls loaded with npks > 0 has picks in the Parquet. The reverse is not quite true: a few station-days the table calls unknown do have picks. They come in blocks on the first days of a shard's 20-day window, which is the signature of a shard preempted on Spot and resumed by another worker: the resuming attempt wrote the manifest, so the days the first attempt finished are absent from it (28_resumed_shard_overwrite.md). So: whether a station-day has picks, ask the Parquet; whether a station-day without picks had data, ask the table.

4. The same month in the 2025 catalogue¶

quakescope-2025/ holds the picks of the 2025 run (Ni et al., 2025): PhaseNet with the instance weights, 2002 to March 2025, converted from the retired database into this layout. Two differences matter before comparing:

  • 2025 picked every band a station offered each day, 2026 only the best one. To compare like with like, keep the 2025 picks on the band 2026 used.
  • 2025 skipped station-days whose data had more than 150 traces and recorded them with zero picks; the 2026 reader merges fragmented days instead.
In [10]:
q_local = mirror("quakescope-2025", NET, YEAR, MONTH)
p25 = read_picks(q_local)
for df in (picks, p25):
    df["date"] = df.peak.dt.floor("D")

bands = p25.groupby(["tid", "date"]).cha.nunique()
print(f"2025: {len(bands):,} station-days, {(bands > 1).mean():.0%} of them picked on more than one band")

band26 = picks.groupby(["tid", "date"]).cha.first().rename("cha26")
p25 = p25.join(band26, on=["tid", "date"])
same = p25[p25.cha == p25.cha26].copy()      # 2025 picks on the band 2026 used, on station-days both picked
print(f"2025 picks on the 2026 band: {len(same):,} of {len(p25):,}")
print(f"stations: 2026 {picks.tid.nunique()}, 2025 {p25.tid.nunique()}, both {len(set(picks.tid) & set(p25.tid))}")

Pick by pick: match each pick to the nearest pick of the same station and phase in the other catalogue, within 0.5 s. The fraction matched, as a function of the pick's own conf, says how much of each catalogue the other one also found; the time differences of matched picks say whether the two weight sets put the arrival in the same place.

In [12]:
def nearest(a, b, tol_s=0.5):
    # For each pick in a, the signed time to the nearest pick in b (same tid, pha), within tol_s.
    a = a.sort_values("peak"); b = b.sort_values("peak")[["tid", "pha", "peak"]].rename(columns={"peak": "peak_b"})
    m = pd.merge_asof(a, b, left_on="peak", right_on="peak_b", by=["tid", "pha"],
                      direction="nearest", tolerance=pd.Timedelta(seconds=tol_s))
    m["dt"] = (m.peak - m.peak_b).dt.total_seconds()
    return m

common = sd[["tid", "date"]].drop_duplicates()
a26 = picks.merge(common, on=["tid", "date"]); a25 = same.merge(common, on=["tid", "date"])
m26, m25 = nearest(a26, a25), nearest(a25, a26)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4))
bins = np.linspace(0.2, 1.0, 17)
for m, c, lab in ((m26, C26, "2026 picks found in 2025"), (m25, C25, "2025 picks found in 2026")):
    for ph, ls in (("P", "-"), ("S", "--")):
        g = m[m.pha == ph]
        frac = g.groupby(pd.cut(g.conf, bins), observed=False).dt.apply(lambda s: s.notna().mean())
        ax[0].plot(0.5 * (bins[1:] + bins[:-1]), frac.values, ls, color=c, lw=1.5, label=f"{lab}, {ph}")
ax[0].set_xlabel("conf of the pick"); ax[0].set_ylabel("fraction matched within 0.5 s"); ax[0].set_ylim(0, 1)
ax[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
for ph, ls in (("P", "-"), ("S", "--")):
    g = m26[(m26.pha == ph) & m26.dt.notna() & (m26.conf >= 0.5)]
    ax[1].hist(g.dt, bins=np.linspace(-0.5, 0.5, 101), histtype="step", ls=ls, lw=1.3, color="#333",
               label=f"{ph}: median {g.dt.median() * 1e3:+.0f} ms, median |dt| {g.dt.abs().median() * 1e3:.0f} ms")
ax[1].set_yscale("log"); ax[1].set_xlabel("2026 minus 2025 arrival time (s), conf >= 0.5")
ax[1].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()

for thr in (0.2, 0.5):
    for ph in "PS":
        x = m26[(m26.pha == ph) & (m26.conf >= thr)]; y = m25[(m25.pha == ph) & (m25.conf >= thr)]
        print(f"conf >= {thr}, {ph}: 2026 {len(x):>9,} picks, {x.dt.notna().mean():.0%} found in 2025 | "
              f"2025 {len(y):>9,} picks, {y.dt.notna().mean():.0%} found in 2026")

conf >= 0.2, P: 2026 2,774,569 picks, 42% found in 2025 | 2025 2,966,993 picks, 39% found in 2026

conf >= 0.2, S: 2026 2,948,305 picks, 29% found in 2025 | 2025 2,053,505 picks, 41% found in 2026

conf >= 0.5, P: 2026 1,336,977 picks, 64% found in 2025 | 2025 1,082,751 picks, 74% found in 2026

conf >= 0.5, S: 2026 1,333,048 picks, 50% found in 2025 | 2025   444,813 picks, 81% found in 2026

What this month shows, measured when the notebook was built (2026-10-19):

  • S picks are where the two runs differ most. At conf >= 0.5 the 2026 run has about three times as many S picks as 2025 on the same station-days and band, and finds about 80 % of the 2025 S picks; 2025 finds about half of the 2026 ones. This is the instance ceiling on dense near-field aftershocks that led us to pick western with original: no threshold recovers it.
  • The two weight sets do not put the arrival in the same place. Matched 2026 picks are later than 2025 picks by about 50 ms (P) and 100 ms (S). This is a property of the weights, not of the clocks: against analyst picks, original is late by +28 ms (P) and +28 ms (S) at Ridgecrest and +20 / +50 ms at Norcia, while instance is early by 10 to 40 ms (docs/benchmark/results/timing_full.csv, median residuals). Do not mix picks from the two catalogues in one location or tomography run without a per-phase correction.
  • On single-component short-period stations the difference reverses. This month of CI is almost all HH. Across every western station-day picked by both runs from 2002 to March 2025, 2026 has a median of 2 to 3 times the 2025 picks on HH, BH and HN, but 0.06 times on EH (5.0 M station-days; docs/paper_2026/figures/numbers.json). The EH stations of NC, UW, CI, MB and NN are mostly vertical-only. Re-picking two NC EHZ station-days locally reproduced both catalogues (23 and 224 picks; 18 and 3,745) and both weight sets recalled the NCEDC analyst picks there; the extra instance picks far exceed what the located seismicity supports (3,745 picks on a day with two NCEDC events within 1 degree). Expect far fewer picks on those stations in 2026, and read the 2025 rates on them as mostly noise.
  • conf is on a different scale in each: 2025 instance scores fewer S picks high. A shared threshold is not a shared operating point.

Read the comparison as a statement about this network and month, not about the weights in general: which catalogue finds more depends on the station, the sequence and the threshold, and the benchmark notebooks score both against analyst picks (benchmark summary). Matching within 0.5 s is a detection test; 2026 picks absent from 2025 are a mixture of arrivals 2025 missed and false detections 2026 made, and only a reference (analyst picks, or an associated catalogue) can split them.

5. Check picks on the waveforms¶

The catalogues store no waveforms. Fetch them from the SCEDC FDSN service with ObsPy, the same data the picker read, and draw both catalogues' picks on top. The station-minute is the busiest one of confident 2026 picks on the mainshock day, 2019-07-06, among those where the 2025 run also has at least three.

In [13]:
import obspy
from obspy.clients.fdsn import Client

def per_minute(df):
    d = df[(df.conf >= 0.5) & (df.date == pd.Timestamp("2019-07-06"))]
    return d.groupby(["tid", d.peak.dt.floor("min").rename("minute")]).size()
both = pd.concat([per_minute(picks).rename("n26"), per_minute(same).rename("n25")], axis=1).dropna()
tid, minute = both[both.n25 >= 3].n26.idxmax()          # busiest 2026 minute where 2025 also has picks
net, sta, loc = tid.split(".")
band = picks.loc[picks.tid == tid, "cha"].iloc[0]
t0 = obspy.UTCDateTime(minute) - 10
st = Client("SCEDC", timeout=60).get_waveforms(network=net, station=sta, location=loc or "--",
                                               channel=f"{band}?", starttime=t0, endtime=t0 + 80)
st.merge(fill_value="interpolate").detrend("demean").filter("bandpass", freqmin=2, freqmax=20)

win = lambda df: df[(df.tid == tid) & (df.peak >= minute - pd.Timedelta(seconds=10)) & (df.peak < minute + pd.Timedelta(seconds=70))]
w26, w25 = win(picks), win(same)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(st), 1, figsize=(12, 1.9 * len(st)), sharex=True)
for ax, tr in zip(np.atleast_1d(axes), st):
    t = tr.times() + (tr.stats.starttime - t0)
    ax.plot(t, tr.data / np.abs(tr.data).max(), lw=0.45, color="#333")
    for df, c, y in ((w26, C26, (0.5, 1)), (w25, C25, (0, 0.5))):
        for _, p in df.iterrows():
            ax.axvline(obspy.UTCDateTime(p.peak) - t0, *y, lw=1.2,
                       ls="-" if p.pha == "P" else "--", color=c)
    ax.set_ylabel(tr.stats.channel)
axes[-1].set_xlabel(f"seconds after {t0.isoformat()}")
axes[0].set_title(f"{tid}: 2026 picks upper half (blue), 2025 lower half (orange); P solid, S dashed "
                  f"({len(w26)} and {len(w25)} picks)", loc="left", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()

6. Ocean-bottom picks¶

obs holds PickBlue picks on ocean-bottom seismometers, offshore stations only, selected per station by a land mask and a water depth of at least 10 m. The example is AACSE (network XO) in August 2018, 67 stations from the Alaska Peninsula to the trench. Its picks were scored against the analyst picks of Barcheck and colleagues: 86 % of analyst P and S arrivals have a PickBlue pick within 1 s (OBS benchmark). OBS days often carry only the short-period EL band, which is picked for this catalogue alone. This month also shows how much duplication an interrupted shard leaves: about a fifth of the rows repeat a pick.

In [14]:
obs = read_picks(mirror("obs", "XO", 2018, 8))
st_o = o.assign(depth_m=-o.elevation)[["id", "latitude", "longitude", "depth_m"]]
per = (obs.groupby("tid").agg(P=("pha", lambda s: (s == "P").sum()), S=("pha", lambda s: (s == "S").sum()),
                              days=("peak", lambda s: s.dt.floor("D").nunique()), band=("cha", "first"))
          .join(st_o.set_index("id")))
per["per_day"] = (per.P + per.S) / per.days

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.4))
sc = ax[0].scatter(per.longitude, per.latitude, c=np.log10(per.per_day), s=28, cmap="viridis")
fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax[0], label="log10 picks per station-day")
ax[0].set_aspect(1 / np.cos(np.radians(55))); ax[0].set_title("XO, August 2018", loc="left", fontsize=10.5)
ax[1].scatter(per.depth_m, per.P / per.days, s=22, color=C26, label="P")
ax[1].scatter(per.depth_m, per.S / per.days, s=22, marker="s", facecolors="none", edgecolors=C25, label="S")
ax[1].set_yscale("log"); ax[1].set_xlabel("water depth (m)"); ax[1].set_ylabel("picks per station-day")
ax[1].legend(frameon=False); ax[1].set_title("P and S rates by water depth", loc="left", fontsize=10.5)
fig.tight_layout()
per.sort_values("per_day", ascending=False).head(8)

On the shelf (the LT stations, about 150 m of water) S rates scatter over two orders of magnitude and often sit far below P; at the deep stations seaward of the trench, S tracks P. Shelf noise and the sediment layer change what a picker sees; the OBS benchmark scores both against analyst picks.

7. Provenance¶

Every pick carries a run id, and the run record names the model, weights, thresholds and library versions. A campaign runs under one configuration but creates a new run id at every worker start, so there are thousands of records that differ only in run_id and created: quote the configuration, not the id.

In [15]:
for cat, df in (("western", picks), ("quakescope-2025", p25), ("obs", obs)):
    rec = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(f"{HTTPS}/{cat}/runs/{df.rid.iloc[0]}.json"))
    keep = {k: rec.get(k) for k in ("model", "weight", "p_threshold", "s_threshold", "components_loaded",
                                    "seisbench_version", "weight_version")}
    print(f"{cat:16s} {df.rid.nunique():5d} run ids this month; {keep}")

8. Reading at scale¶

One network-month is a few million picks and reads in a second once mirrored. The catalogues are not: western is 580,407 objects. What costs time is the number of files touched, not bytes.

  1. Put the partition in the path. picks/network=CI/year=2019/month=07/*.parquet lists a few hundred objects. A glob over picks/** with a WHERE network = 'CI' lists all 580,407 before pruning anything (measured: not back after 7 minutes).
  2. For more than a month, mirror first. aws s3 sync --no-sign-request or s3fs.get(recursive=True) land at 15 to 20 MB/s; a network-year of western is about 1 GB, the whole of western 55.3 GB.
  3. Aggregate in the engine, read only the columns you need, and de-duplicate in the same query.
aws s3 sync --no-sign-request s3://quakescope-picks-2026/western/picks/network=UW/year=2019/ \
    quakescope_mirror/western/picks/network=UW/year=2019/

DuckDB over the local mirror, de-duplicating with DISTINCT ON:

In [16]:
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()
t0 = time.time()
top = con.sql(f'''
    WITH p AS (
        SELECT DISTINCT ON (tid, cha, pha, peak) tid, pha, conf
        FROM read_parquet('{MIRROR}/western/picks/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = 1)
    )
    SELECT tid, count(*) AS picks, count(*) FILTER (pha = 'S') AS s_picks, round(avg(conf), 3) AS mean_conf
    FROM p GROUP BY tid ORDER BY picks DESC LIMIT 8
''').df()
print(f"{time.time() - t0:.2f} s against the local mirror")
top

9. Next¶

  • A region and a period, with coverage from the availability table and export for an associator: download_the_catalogue.ipynb.
  • Association. These are per-station picks, not events. PyOcto, GaMMA, GENIE or VORA turn them into a catalogue; seisbench_pyocto_ncedc.ipynb shows the input shape.
  • Thresholds. Everything at or above 0.2 is stored. Choose your own floor on your own events; at a matched number of picks the land weight sets are within a few points of each other on analyst picks, at a shared threshold they are not.
  • Known limits. One band per station-day in 2026 (a station with HH and HN was picked on HH). amp exists only above conf 0.5. Networks our EarthScope account may not read (TD, EO, LH in western; NV in obs) are absent. 1,030 western station-days (1,010 on SF, 20 on X7) are recorded unread, too_big: day files that crash the miniSEED decoder or exceed 4 GB.
  • Citing. Cite the repository (CITATION.cff) and Ni et al. (2025, doi:10.26443/seismica.v4i2.1738), name the prefix, and give the date you read it. A DOI for the 2026 catalogues is in preparation.
  • Problems, gaps, requests: https://github.com/SeisSCOPED/QuakeScope/issues.
